title: The Sealed Train and the Glass Case: Simbirsk, the Emigration, and the State That Kept the Body
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Simbirsk, the birth house on Streletskaya
stops.date_confidence: attested. Both calendars are given in the encyclopedic sources: 22 April 1870 New Style, 10 April Old Style. The Streletskaya birth house is preserved as its own museum, opened 16 April 1970, and is a different building from both the Lenin Memorial complex and the Moskovskaya Street family house-museum where the Ulyanovs lived from 1878; the research pool conflated all three and the conflation is corrected here.
stops.campa: In a wooden house on Streletskaya Street, in a provincial town strung along the right bank of the Volga, Maria Alexandrovna Ulyanova bears her third child on the twenty-second of April. The father, Ilya Nikolayevich, is inspector of public schools for Simbirsk province, a state servant climbing toward hereditary nobility by examination and diligence. The boy is registered Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov. The family will move to a house of its own on Moskovskaya Street eight years later. The town keeps two calendars, Julian for its own business and Gregorian for the world outside. The same day is the tenth of April.
suggested_refs: The house-museum Dom, gde rodilsya V. I. Lenin, Streletskaya Street, Ulyanovsk

stops.name: Simbirsk, the gymnasium and the inspector's death
stops.date_confidence: attested for the gymnasium record, the gold medal, and the death by cerebral hemorrhage in January 1886; the day within January is not fixed by the pool's sources and the date here orders the segment. Ilya Ulyanov is buried in the Pokrovsky necropolis, not at the house; the pool staged a separate grave stop with coordinates identical to the birth house, which is why it has been folded in here instead.
stops.campa: He goes through the classical gymnasium at the head of every class, Latin and Greek his strongest subjects, under a headmaster named Fyodor Kerensky, whose own son will one day hold Russia for eight months and lose it to him. In January 1886 Ilya Ulyanov dies suddenly of a cerebral hemorrhage, thirty years of service ending in an afternoon. The widow is left with six children and a pension. Vladimir is fifteen. He finishes the gymnasium in 1887 with the gold medal, and Kerensky writes him a leaving testimonial praising his conduct.
suggested_refs: Fyodor Kerensky's leaving testimonial for the pupil Ulyanov, Simbirsk gymnasium, 1887

stops.name: Simbirsk, the news from Shlisselburg
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrest, trial, and hanging of Alexander Ulyanov at Shlisselburg Fortress on 20 May 1887. The scene is staged in Simbirsk, where Vladimir was, and not at the fortress, which is Alexander's place. The celebrated reply attributed to Vladimir on hearing the news, that we shall not take that road, is a later hagiographic formula by scholarly consensus and is not securely contemporaneous; it is therefore not quoted.
stops.campa: Alexander Ulyanov, the eldest son, a biology student in Petersburg, is taken in March with the remnant of a Narodnaya Volya circle carrying bombs built into hollowed medical dictionaries, meant for Alexander III on the anniversary of his father's assassination. He refuses to petition for mercy. On the twentieth of May he is hanged in the fortress at Shlisselburg with four others. The news reaches the house in Simbirsk where Vladimir, seventeen, is sitting his final examinations. Neighbours stop calling at the door. The family leaves the province.
suggested_refs: The Shlisselburg Fortress execution register, 20 May 1887
Anna Ulyanova's memoir of the family in 1887

segments.name: Kazan, Kokushkino, and the Law Nobody Taught Him

stops.name: Kazan University, the law faculty and the protest
stops.date_confidence: attested for enrolment in August 1887 and for arrest and expulsion in December 1887 after a student protest; the day of enrolment is not fixed and defaults to the first.
stops.campa: In August he enters the law faculty at Kazan, four months after his brother's hanging and with the police already holding a file on the family name. In December the students gather over a petition against the new university statutes; Ulyanov is in the hall. He is arrested the same night, expelled, struck off the register, and put out of the city under police supervision. His university education has lasted a single term, and the ministry ledger now carries him under a standing description: brother of a hanged man, unreliable. He leaves Kazan without a degree and without the right to sit for one.
suggested_refs: The Kazan University disciplinary file on the student Ulyanov, December 1887

stops.name: Kokushkino, the year under supervision
stops.date_confidence: attested for the confinement at the family estate under open police supervision through 1888; the day is an ordering device. Coordinates corrected: the pool gave 55.9333 / 48.8167, some 55 km west of the true site. The estate, now Lenino-Kokushkino in Pestrechinsky District, Tatarstan, is at 55.817 / 49.683. The reading order, Chernyshevsky then Marx, is standard biography rather than a documented sequence.
stops.campa: The estate at Kokushkino came into the family through his mother's father, the physician Alexander Blank. Here Ulyanov is held for a year under open police supervision, forbidden the capitals, his sister Anna under the same order in the same house. He reads through the shelves and the back numbers of the thick journals, Chernyshevsky first and then, in earnest, Marx. His mother writes petition after petition for his readmission to a university, any university in the empire. Every petition is refused.
suggested_refs: The Blank family estate at Kokushkino, now Lenino-Kokushkino, Tatarstan

stops.name: St Petersburg, the external examinations
stops.date_confidence: attested with a contradiction inside the research pool, resolved here. One lens dated the degree May 1890, which is the month his mother won him permission to sit externally, not the month he sat. He took the examinations in two rounds, autumn 1890 and spring 1891, and the first-class diploma was issued in November 1891. The day within November is not fixed.
stops.campa: Barred from every faculty in the empire, he prepares the whole four-year law course alone, out of borrowed texts, in Samara and Kazan. In May 1890 his mother wins him permission to sit as an external candidate of the University of St Petersburg. He takes the examinations in two rounds, autumn and spring, among men he has never studied beside. He has attended no lecture in the subject and belonged to no faculty. The first-class diploma of the University of St Petersburg is issued to him in November 1891, four years and one term after the police put him out of Kazan.
suggested_refs: The external-candidate examination register of the University of St Petersburg, 1890-1891

stops.name: Samara, Khardin's chambers and the linden avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested that he practised as assistant to the barrister Andrei Khardin in Samara in 1892-1893 and that the family held the Alakaevka smallholding from 1889; the character of the docket is standard biography, and the day is an ordering device. Alakaevka, at roughly 53.0833 / 50.6167, is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: He is admitted to the bar as assistant to Andrei Khardin, a Samara barrister and a strong chess player, and for something over a year practises law: petty theft, assault, a dispute over a horse, defendants who mostly plead guilty and are mostly convicted. Between dockets the family keeps a smallholding at Alakaevka, and there, walking the linden avenue, he works through Capital and argues down the Narodnik faith that the peasant commune can carry Russia past capitalism without passing through it. In 1893 he closes the practice.
suggested_refs: The Alakaevka smallholding, Samara province, where he read Capital
Khardin's Samara chambers and the surviving case list

segments.name: The Circles, the Cell, and the Yenisei

stops.name: St Petersburg, the workers' circles beyond the Nevsky Gate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to St Petersburg in autumn 1893 and for the formation of the League of Struggle in 1895; the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He arrives in the capital in the autumn of 1893, twenty-three years old, a barrister on paper and a Marxist in fact, and finds the propaganda circles already running in the mills beyond the Nevsky Gate. He teaches political economy to weavers and metalworkers, writes leaflets about fines and hours in language the shop floor will read, and argues against those who would keep the work industrial that a strike over kopecks and a war on the autocracy are one struggle at two distances. In 1895 the circles combine as the League of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class.
suggested_refs: The 1895 leaflets of the League of Struggle for the Emancipation of the Working Class

stops.name: Shpalernaya Street, the House of Preliminary Detention
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrest of 20 December 1895 Old Style and for roughly fourteen months in the House of Preliminary Detention on Shpalernaya Street. Coordinates corrected: the pool's 59.9494 / 30.3269 lies west of the street's western end; the prison at Shpalernaya 25 is at approximately 59.9476 / 30.3565. The milk-ink letters are traditional, resting on Krupskaya's memoir rather than a document.
stops.campa: On the night of the twentieth of December the police take the League apart, some forty arrests, the first number of its newspaper still in proof. Ulyanov spends fourteen months in the pretrial prison on Shpalernaya Street awaiting a sentence that requires no trial: administrative exile, decided in an office by men he never sees. He works. Books come in from the Free Economic Society library; chapters of The Development of Capitalism in Russia go out. So do letters written in milk between the lines of a legal text, the writing read by holding the page to a lamp.
suggested_refs: The House of Preliminary Detention, Shpalernaya 25, St Petersburg
Krupskaya's account of the milk-ink correspondence

stops.name: Shushenskoye, three years on the Yenisei
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sentence of three years' administrative exile handed down in February 1897 and served at Shushenskoye in the Minusinsk district; the arrival month is approximate and the day is an ordering device. The state stipend and the daily routine are standard biography.
stops.campa: The sentence is three years in Eastern Siberia, and the district chosen is mild by the standards of the system: Shushenskoye, a village of a few hundred souls where the Shush comes down into the Yenisei, steppe and pine and a good dry climate. The state pays him eight roubles a month, enough for board, milk, and a hunting dog. He shoots duck, skates the river, translates the Webbs with Krupskaya, and finishes the book he began in the cell. Exiles a hundred versts apart write to each other as though they were holding a congress.
suggested_refs: The Development of Capitalism in Russia, completed in exile and published 1899

stops.name: Shushenskoye, the Orthodox marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested that the marriage took place at Shushenskoye in July 1898 and that a church ceremony was the legal condition of Krupskaya's transfer to his place of exile. Contradiction not resolved: one encyclopedic source gives 10 July 1898, another 22 July 1898, a gap consistent with Old Style against New Style, but no source in the pool says which reading is which.
stops.campa: Nadezhda Konstantinovna Krupskaya, arrested in the same sweep and sentenced to Ufa, petitions to serve her term at Shushenskoye instead, on the ground that she is his fiancee. The authorities grant it on one condition: that they marry at once, and in church. Neither believes a word of the service. They are married in the village church in the summer of 1898, her mother in the house and the district officer's written permission in the drawer. That same week she takes over his correspondence. She will still be doing it twenty-six years later, in the weeks before he dies.
suggested_refs: The Shushenskoye parish marriage register, July 1898

segments.name: Iskra: the Paper, the Clause, and the Split

stops.name: Munich, the spark on thin paper
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Munich editorial base from September 1900 under the cover name Meyer. Corrected against the pool, which said the paper was launched from Munich in September: issue number one was printed in Leipzig, dated 1 December 1900 in some sources and 11 December in others, and appeared on 24 December. Nothing was printed in Munich in September. The pseudonym Lenin first appears in print in December 1901 and its origin is unresolved.
stops.campa: His term ends in 1900 and he leaves the empire, because the paper he means to make cannot be made inside it. In Munich, under the cover name Meyer, he sets up a board with Plekhanov, Martov, Axelrod, Zasulich, and Potresov: a newspaper printed abroad on paper thin enough to sew into a coat lining, run in through the Baltic ports, meant to give a hundred scattered committees one line, one argument, and one register of who is who. Issue number one is printed in Leipzig and appears at the end of December.
stops.quote: A newspaper is not only a collective propagandist and a collective agitator, it is also a collective organiser.
stops.quote_source: Where to Begin?, Iskra, May 1901, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: Iskra No. 1, Leipzig, December 1900

stops.name: London, the organisation of revolutionaries
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to London in April 1902, for the publication of What Is to Be Done? in March 1902, and for the Second Congress of the RSDLP opening in Brussels in July 1903 and finishing in London. Corrected against the pool, which gave London as the place of publication: the pamphlet is a J. H. W. Dietz imprint from Stuttgart and was out a month before he reached England. The stop is dated to the congress and covers both.
stops.campa: Bavarian police close on the Iskra office and the board moves to London in April 1902, a month after Dietz of Stuttgart issues the pamphlet that will divide Russian socialism. What Is to Be Done? argues that workers left to themselves arrive at trade-union consciousness and go no further, and that the rest has to be carried to them by a party of professionals. He reads in the British Museum, in the room where Karl Marx wrote. In the summer of 1903 the congress, opened in Brussels and finished here, breaks in two over a clause defining who is a member. His side is the majority, bolshinstvo, and keeps the name.
stops.quote: Give us an organisation of revolutionaries, and we will overturn Russia
stops.quote_source: What Is To Be Done? (1902), ch. 4, Marxists Internet Archive; Lenin frames it as varying a well-known statement, an Archimedes allusion
suggested_refs: What Is to Be Done?, J. H. W. Dietz, Stuttgart, March 1902
The Reading Room of the British Museum, used by Marx and by Lenin in turn
Karl Marx's grave at Highgate Cemetery, London
sources: marxists.org, What Is To Be Done?

stops.name: Geneva, the board he loses
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Iskra board relocated to Geneva and that Lenin lost control of the paper after the congress; the month is approximate and the day is an ordering device. The social detail of the emigre colony is traditional.
stops.campa: The board moves to Geneva and he moves with it. Plekhanov, wanting the old six editors restored, hands the paper back to the men Lenin has just defeated at the congress, and before the year is out the founder of Iskra is off its board. He starts a paper of his own. The split that began as a clause in a draft constitution goes down into the households: the Russian colony divides by which cafe it drinks in, and men who edited the same page for three years pass each other on the quay without speaking.
suggested_refs: The 1903 minutes of the Second Congress of the RSDLP

stops.name: St Petersburg, the return in the year of revolution
stops.date_confidence: attested for Bloody Sunday in January 1905 and for the clandestine return to St Petersburg in November 1905 after the October Manifesto; the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Bloody Sunday in January, a crowd at the Winter Palace with a petition and ikons, and the volleys; by autumn the empire is in general strike and the tsar has conceded a manifesto. He comes back in November, illegally, under a false name, to a city where soviets have appeared without anybody's instruction and the Bolsheviks are arguing whether to enter them. He tells them to enter, and to arm. He writes in the legal press for six weeks. By December the Moscow rising is broken and the police are at the door again.
stops.quote: Religion is opium for the people. Religion is a sort of spiritual booze, in which the slaves of capital drown their human image, their demand for a life more or less worthy of man.
stops.quote_source: Socialism and Religion, Novaya Zhizn, 3 December 1905, Marxists Internet Archive; the condensed form in circulation, religion is the opium of the people, is Marx's phrasing and not this sentence
suggested_refs: Novaya Zhizn, the legal Bolshevik daily of late 1905

stops.name: Tampere, the Workers' Hall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Bolshevik conference at Tampere in December 1905 and the first meeting with Stalin there are widely reported in tertiary sources, but the verification pass could not confirm them from a primary or scholarly source: the Wikipedia page 'Lenin Museum, Tampere' returned 404. Carried at R and flagged rather than dropped.
stops.campa: The Bolshevik conference meets in December in the red brick Workers' Hall of a Finnish mill town, inside the Grand Duchy, where Russian police operate only by permission. Here, the accounts hold, he meets for the first time a Georgian delegate travelling as Ivanovich, whom the world will learn to call Stalin. The conference sits to debate boycotting the Duma and hears, in mid-session, that the Moscow rising has failed. It converts itself into a discussion of how to retreat, and sends the delegates home.
suggested_refs: The Tampere Workers' Hall, venue of the December 1905 Bolshevik conference
sources: Dossier synthesis, standard biography; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Kuokkala, the Bolshevik Centre in the Grand Duchy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the retreat into Finland in 1906 and for the Bolshevik command post at Kuokkala; the month is approximate. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 60.1725 / 29.75: Kuokkala, renamed Repino in 1948, is at 60.167 / 29.867. The Tiflis expropriation of 1907 is carried at R, the verification pass having failed to obtain a primary or academic source for it.
stops.campa: Reaction closes over the empire and he crosses into Finland, to a dacha at Kuokkala an hour by train from the capital and legally outside it. From here the faction is run: couriers in and out daily, the Bolshevik Centre meeting in the rooms upstairs, and the expropriations that pay for all of it sanctioned in those rooms while the party congress condemns them on paper downstairs. In 1907 Kamo's men take something like three hundred and forty-one thousand roubles from a bank convoy in a Tiflis square. Bystanders die in the street.
suggested_refs: The 1907 Tiflis expropriation and the London congress resolution against expropriations
sources: Dossier synthesis for the Tiflis robbery, not re-verified

stops.name: Capri, chess on Gorky's terrace
stops.date_confidence: attested in standard biography (Service) for the 1908 visit to Gorky on Capri during the rupture with Bogdanov's Machist circle; the month and day are ordering devices and the villa itself was not re-verified, the coordinate being for Capri town. Materialism and Empirio-Criticism is dated 1908-09 at R. Lenin's verdict on Sorel is carried from georges_sorel.journey.json, which records that Lenin had read him and dismissed him privately as a muddler.
stops.campa: Gorky keeps a villa on Capri and a household of exiles inside it, and invites the faction's quarrelling philosophers to settle the quarrel in the sun. Lenin comes, plays chess on the terrace, walks the cliff path, and settles nothing. Bogdanov's attempt to fit Marxism to Mach's physics he treats as a theological error requiring a book, and writes the book: Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, hundreds of pages against a friend. He has also read Georges Sorel, who will shortly call him the greatest theorist socialism has had since Marx. His verdict on Sorel is one word. A muddler.
suggested_refs: Materialism and Empirio-Criticism (1909), against Bogdanov and the Machists
Sorel's own judgement on Lenin, Boulogne-sur-Seine, November 1917

stops.name: Paris, a foul hole
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Paris years from December 1908 to 1912 and for his own description of the city. The pin is the canonical corpus Paris coordinate inherited from karl_marx, mikhail_bakunin, jean_paul_sartre, and albert_camus, in preference to the specific Rue Beaunier coordinate 48.8248 / 2.3311; the street is named in the prose instead.
stops.campa: The emigration follows the board to Paris at the end of 1908 and he takes rooms off the Rue Beaunier in the fourteenth arrondissement, out by the old fortifications, with a reading ticket for the Bibliotheque Nationale. Four years pass there, spent quarrelling over party money held in trust by German trustees, over the Caucasian expropriations, over whether to sit in the Duma at all and whether the men who sit there are still socialists. Inessa Armand arrives in 1910 and does not leave the circle again. His own description of the city, written down at the time, is a foul hole.
suggested_refs: The Lenin rooms off the Rue Beaunier, fourteenth arrondissement, Paris

stops.name: Longjumeau, the party school
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool tagged this reconstruction for want of a fetched source; the Wikipedia article on Longjumeau documents the school directly, with eighteen students, fifty-six lectures by Lenin, and the teaching staff named, so the tag is raised to attested. Coordinates corrected from 48.6931 / 2.3086, about a kilometre east of the town, to 48.6943 / 2.2958. The month is approximate for a summer school.
stops.campa: Fourteen kilometres south of Paris, in a village on the Yvette with a tannery and one long street, the faction rents rooms and opens a school. Eighteen students come out of Russia by underground routes, most of them workers, and are billeted on the local people. Lenin delivers fifty-six of the lectures himself, on political economy and the agrarian question; Semashko, Riazanov, Rappoport, Lunacharsky, and Inessa Armand take the rest. In the autumn the students go back over the frontier one at a time, carrying nothing written down.
suggested_refs: The Longjumeau party school of 1911 and its student list

stops.name: Prague, the conference of fourteen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from standard biographical consensus, not independently re-fetched in verification: the Prague Conference of January 1912 constituted the Bolsheviks as an independent party. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He calls a conference in Prague in January 1912 and invites the delegates he wants at it. Fourteen voting members come, all but two of them his own; the Mensheviks are not there, nor the conciliators, nor Trotsky's group, none of them having been asked. By the end of the week the conference has declared itself the party of Russian social democracy, elected a Central Committee, and expelled everyone absent from it. The hall is rented and the city is Austrian. Every socialist outside the room calls the thing a usurpation and goes on saying so in print for years.
suggested_refs: The resolutions of the Prague Conference, January 1912

stops.name: Krakow, Pravda across the border
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to Krakow in 1912 to be nearer the Russian frontier and for the quarrels with Pravda's editors over their moderation. The founding of Pravda in St Petersburg in May 1912 is carried at reconstruction. The month is approximate.
stops.campa: Galicia is Austrian, the frontier is a few hours away, and the Russian post comes in daily; he moves to Krakow to run the party from inside Poland rather than from behind the Alps. A legal daily called Pravda is printing in St Petersburg now, and he writes for it constantly and fights with its editors constantly, because they cut his attacks on the Mensheviks to keep the paper alive under the censor. Six Bolshevik deputies sit in the Fourth Duma and travel to Krakow for their instructions.
suggested_refs: The Krakow correspondence with the Pravda editorial board, 1912-1914

stops.name: Bialy Dunajec, the summers under the Tatras
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summers of 1913 and 1914 in a rented holiday house at Bialy Dunajec near Zakopane, for the party meetings at a Poronin inn, and for the police search of the house on 7 August 1914. The month here orders the first summer.
stops.campa: For two summers he and Krupskaya take a peasant house at Bialy Dunajec below Zakopane, walking in the Tatras, working at a table by the window, drinking at an inn in the neighbouring village of Poronin where the party's meetings are held. Her goitre is treated in Bern. Her mother lives with them. The mountains, he writes home, are excellent. On the seventh of August 1914 the Austrian gendarmerie searches the house and finds notebooks full of statistical tables in a script the searchers cannot read.
suggested_refs: The Poronin inn, meeting place of the Bolshevik Central Committee in 1913

stops.name: Nowy Targ, the enemy alien
stops.date_confidence: attested with a contradiction between the pool's own lenses, resolved here against the geography lens. The Wikipedia article 'Poronin' puts the arrest at Poronin; 'Revolutionary activity of Vladimir Lenin' states he was arrested in Nowy Targ. The reconciliation, that the Bialy Dunajec house was searched and he was then taken to and held at Nowy Targ, is this file's and not a source's. The length of detention, usually given as eleven days, is not confirmed here and is softened in the prose.
stops.campa: Austria-Hungary has been at war with Russia for three days, and the man in the peasant house is a Russian subject carrying tables of figures that the gendarmes read as cipher. He is taken down to the district gaol at Nowy Targ and held there with common prisoners for less than a fortnight, writing petitions for his fellow inmates in the exercise yard. Victor Adler goes to the Austrian minister of the interior and vouches for the prisoner as the most determined enemy of the Russian government now living. He is released, and deported to Switzerland.
suggested_refs: Victor Adler's intercession with the Austrian Ministry of the Interior, August 1914

stops.name: Zimmerwald, the ornithological society
stops.date_confidence: attested for the conference of 5-8 September 1915 at the Hotel Beau Sejour and for the Zimmerwald Left. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 46.8564 / 7.5069, about 4.5 km off: Zimmerwald, merged into the municipality of Wald in Canton Bern in 2003, is at 46.883 / 7.467. The hotel's main building was demolished in the 1960s. The Kienthal conference of 24-30 April 1916, at roughly 46.586 / 7.68, is named here rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: The delegates, very nearly the whole international opposition to the war, ride out of Bern in horse-drawn carriages to a village hotel and register themselves as an ornithological society. What Lenin puts to the conference is not peace. It is that socialists in every country should work for the defeat of their own government and turn the imperialist war into a civil war. He is outvoted, signs the manifesto anyway, and gathers the minority who agree with him into a caucus called the Zimmerwald Left. A second conference at Kienthal the following April moves a little his way.
suggested_refs: The Zimmerwald Manifesto, September 1915
The Kienthal Conference, 24-30 April 1916, attended with Zinoviev and Inessa Armand

stops.name: Zurich, two rooms on the Spiegelgasse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Spiegelgasse residence is documented throughout the secondary literature and is a standard stop on Zurich Lenin tours, but the verification pass could not retrieve a source page for it: the Wikipedia article on the street returned 404. The sausage-factory detail and the January 1917 remark to the Swiss workers are traditional. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Two rooms in a shoemaker's house on a narrow lane in the old town, above a sausage factory whose smell comes up the stairwell; the rent is low, the cantonal library is close, and the war is in its third year. He writes Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, and reads Hegel's Logic with a pencil. In January 1917 he tells an audience of Swiss workers that the older men of his generation may not live to see the decisive battles of the coming revolution. He is forty-six years old. The February telegrams from Petrograd arrive six weeks later.
suggested_refs: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, written in Zurich, 1916
The Spiegelgasse lodgings in Zurich's old town
sources: Standard biographical consensus; the specific source page could not be retrieved

segments.name: 1917: the Carriage, the Station, the Palace

stops.name: Zurich Hauptbahnhof, the carriage that was not sealed
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a calendar error in the pool corrected here. The pool dated the departure 27 March 1917, which is the Old Style date, while dating the arrival at Finland Station 16 April New Style, putting twenty days between two ends of an eight-day journey. Switzerland kept the Gregorian calendar: the train left Zurich on 9 April 1917 New Style, 27 March Old Style. That the carriage was not in fact sealed, the passengers disembarking overnight in Frankfurt, is attested.
stops.campa: The February revolution takes the emigration completely by surprise and then strands it: the Entente will not pass a defeatist through its lines, and Germany will, for reasons of its own that require no explaining. Fritz Platten negotiates the terms. The travellers board at Zurich on the ninth of April, extraterritorial in law, three of the carriage's four doors locked, a chalk line drawn on the floor to divide Russian ground from German. Three doors are not four, and the carriage is not sealed. At Frankfurt the passengers disembark overnight.
stops.quote: not the slightest concession to 'revolutionary defencism' is permissible
stops.quote_source: The Tasks of the Proletariat in the Present Revolution (April Theses), 1917, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: Fritz Platten's agreement with the German legation, Bern, April 1917

stops.name: Finland Station, the ten theses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival on 16 April 1917 New Style, 3 April Old Style, at Finland Station. Whether the April Theses were first read that night or the following day is not settled by the pool's sources and is carried at reconstruction.
stops.campa: He arrives on the evening of the sixteenth to searchlights, a guard of honour from the Baltic Fleet, an armoured car, and a speech of welcome from the Petrograd Soviet's Menshevik chairman urging him to help defend the revolution against all comers. He answers the crowd and not the chairman. The next day he reads ten theses to the Bolshevik delegates: no support for the Provisional Government, no defencism, no parliamentary republic, all power to the Soviets. His own party's newspaper prints them over a note explaining that they are his personal opinion.
stops.quote: No support for the Provisional Government; the utter falsity of all its promises should be made clear, particularly of those relating to the renunciation of annexations.
stops.quote_source: The Tasks of the Proletariat in the Present Revolution (April Theses), 1917, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: Pravda's disclaimer accompanying the first publication of the April Theses

stops.name: Razliv, the hut of hay and branches
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the flight itself, attested for the site. Two corrections to the pool: the hiding place was at 60.0819 / 30.0311 in Sestroretsk, Kurortny District, not the pool's 60.1897 / 29.7897 some 24 km away, and it was in Russia at the time, not Finland. He crossed into Finland only after leaving Razliv in late July. The hut was built by the Bolshevik worker Nikolai Emelianov. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The July demonstrations collapse, the government publishes the charge that he is paid by the German general staff, and Kerensky's police come for him. He shaves the beard, puts on a wig, and is taken out to the marshes by Sestroretsk, where a worker named Nikolai Emelianov hides him and Zinoviev first in a shed and then in a hut of hay and cut branches by Lake Razliv. He is entered in the local reckoning as a Finnish mower. He works there on the book about the state, and crosses into Finland in the autumn.
stops.quote: So long as the state exists there is no freedom. When there is freedom, there will be no state.
stops.quote_source: The State and Revolution (1917), ch. 5, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: Lenin's Hovel, Sestroretsk, the reconstructed hut by Lake Razliv
The State and Revolution, begun at Razliv and continued in Finland

stops.name: The Smolny Institute, the command post
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Smolny Institute served as Bolshevik headquarters from October 1917 and that Lenin lived and governed from its rooms until March 1918. The date is Old Style, as the insurrection is universally dated in the sources; the equivalent is 6 November 1917 New Style.
stops.campa: He comes back into the capital in October under a wig and a workman's cap, argues the Central Committee into a vote for insurrection against two members who then publish their dissent in a paper that is not the party's, and installs himself in a girls' boarding school on the eastern edge of the city. The Military Revolutionary Committee works out of the same corridors. On the night of the twenty-fourth, small parties take the telephone exchange, the telegraph, the bridges, and the railway stations, mostly without firing.
suggested_refs: The Smolny Institute, headquarters of the Military Revolutionary Committee, October 1917

stops.name: The Winter Palace, the ministers written down
stops.date_confidence: attested; 7 November 1917 New Style, 25-26 October Old Style, both calendars given in the sources. The Second Congress of Soviets elected the Council of People's Commissars with Lenin as chairman the following day.
stops.campa: The palace holds out for a day behind a barricade of firewood, defended by officer cadets, a bicycle detachment, and a women's battalion. The Aurora fires a blank. The guns of the Peter and Paul fortress fire live and mostly miss. Late in the night men come in through service doors nobody has locked, find the cabinet sitting at a table in the Malachite Room, and write their names down on a sheet of paper. Across the river the Second Congress of Soviets is in session; the Mensheviks walk out of it, and the delegates who stay ratify a transfer of power that has already happened.
suggested_refs: The protocol of arrest of the Provisional Government, Malachite Room, 26 October 1917 O.S.
The Second Congress of Soviets and the election of Sovnarkom, 8 November 1917

stops.name: The Tauride Palace, the assembly that met once
stops.date_confidence: attested for the dates of 18-19 January 1918 and for the dispersal; the narrative detail is carried at reconstruction from standard histories. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 59.9469 / 30.3831, about 450 m southeast of the building, to 59.9478 / 30.3758. The founding of the Cheka under Dzerzhinsky on 20 December 1917 is carried at reconstruction.
stops.campa: The Constituent Assembly that every Russian party has demanded for a generation is elected in November, and gives the Socialist Revolutionaries more than twice the Bolshevik vote. It meets once, on the eighteenth of January, in the hall where the Duma used to sit, and refuses to endorse the Soviet decrees. The Cheka has existed since December. At four in the morning the sailor commanding the guard informs the chairman that the guard is tired and the hall must be cleared. The delegates go out into the street, and the Congress of Soviets meets in their place. The Constituent Assembly does not sit a second time.
stops.quote: only communism makes the state absolutely unnecessary, for there is nobody to be suppressed
stops.quote_source: The State and Revolution (1917), ch. 5, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: The single session of the All-Russian Constituent Assembly, Tauride Palace, 18-19 January 1918
sources: Standard histories of the Constituent Assembly

segments.name: The State: Peace, Terror, and the Bullet

stops.name: Brest-Litovsk, the obscene peace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the treaty of 3 March 1918 and for the losses it imposed: roughly 34 per cent of population, 54 per cent of industrial land, 89 per cent of coalfields, 26 per cent of railways. Lenin never travelled to Brest-Litovsk; the delegation signed there and he fought the ratification battle in Petrograd and Moscow. The stop is kept because the act is his, and the absence is stated here rather than hidden.
stops.campa: He is not in the fortress town when the treaty is signed, and he has spent four months forcing his own party to accept it, against the Left Communists who want a revolutionary war and against Trotsky, who wants neither war nor peace and offers that formula to the Germans, who answer it by advancing. The terms cost a third of the population, half the industrial land, nine tenths of the coal. A state with no army, he argues, has nothing to pay with except ground, and Germany's own revolution will cancel the debt. He wins the ratification and keeps the word he has used for the thing all along. An obscene peace.
stops.quote: politics begin where millions of men and women are; where there are not thousands, but millions, that is where serious politics begin
stops.quote_source: Political Report of the Central Committee, Extraordinary Seventh Congress of the R.C.P.(B.), 7 March 1918, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, 3 March 1918
The ratification debate at the Seventh Congress of the R.C.P.(B.), March 1918
sources: marxists.org, Political Report of the Central Committee, 7 March 1918

stops.name: The Moscow Kremlin, the capital moves inland
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exact date of the move, attested that the capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in March 1918 and that Lenin governed from Kremlin quarters as chairman of Sovnarkom until May 1923. The pin is the canonical Kremlin coordinate inherited from h_g_wells.journey.json.
stops.campa: Petrograd is a hundred and fifty versts from the German line and cannot be held, so in March the government moves inland to the old capital it has spent its whole life despising, and the men who made a revolution against the autocracy take up residence inside the autocracy's fortress. He has three rooms in the Senate building, a small study, a kitchen shared with his sister. Sovnarkom meets down the corridor to an agenda he keeps to the minute, fining latecomers. He will govern from behind these walls for five years and leave them for the last time in May 1923.
suggested_refs: Lenin's study and living quarters in the Senate building of the Moscow Kremlin
The killing of Nicholas II and his family at the Ipatiev House, Ekaterinburg, 17 July 1918: no surviving signed instruction links Lenin to the order, and the command chain remains undocumented

stops.name: Penza, the telegram of the eleventh of August
stops.date_confidence: attested. Lenin never travelled to Penza; this is the place the order targeted. Provenance flagged: the Library of Congress exhibit page holding the translation returned HTTP 403 at verification and web.archive.org was blocked, so the text was confirmed against the Wikipedia article 'Lenin's hanging order', which reproduces the LOC translation in full and cites it. Nobody in this pipeline read the LOC page directly. The Library of Congress rendering has hundreds of verst, singular.
stops.campa: A rising of peasants against grain requisition breaks out in the Penza district in August, and the local committee telegraphs Moscow for instructions. The answer is signed by the chairman of the Council of People's Commissars in person: four numbered points and a postscript, addressed to Kurayev, Bosch, Minkin and the other Penza communists. Publish their names. Seize all their grain. Designate hostages. The first of the four points is the hanging. The document is left out of the Soviet editions of his collected works for seventy years and comes out of the archive after 1991.
stops.quote: Hang (absolutely hang, in full view of the people) no fewer than one hundred known kulaks, fatcats, bloodsuckers. ... Do it in such a fashion that for hundreds of verst around the people see, tremble, know, shout: the bloodsucking kulaks are being strangled and will be strangled. ... Yours, Lenin. P.S. Find some truly hard men.
stops.quote_source: Telegram to the Penza Gubernia Executive Committee, 11 August 1918, Library of Congress translation as reproduced in the Wikipedia article 'Lenin's hanging order'; the ellipses cover points 2 to 4 of the four-point order and the closing instruction to telegraph receipt and implementation
suggested_refs: The Library of Congress exhibit 'The Struggle Against the Peasantry', which displays the telegram
sources: Library of Congress exhibit, cited but not directly reachable (HTTP 403)

stops.name: The Michelson plant, two bullets in the yard
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the pool's plant name corrected. The shooting took place at the Michelson works, Partiyny pereulok 1, Zamoskvorechye, later renamed the Moscow Electromechanical Plant named after Vladimir Ilyich. The Hammer and Sickle works is a different Moscow factory entirely, the former Guzhon metallurgical plant, and the error comes from the Wikipedia article on Fanny Kaplan. Coordinates corrected from 55.7112 / 37.6506 to 55.7208 / 37.63.
stops.campa: He speaks at factories on Fridays without a guard, which the party has repeatedly told him to stop doing. On the thirtieth of August, having spoken in the grenade shop of the Michelson works in Zamoskvorechye, he walks out to the car in the yard and a woman shoots him twice, in the neck and in the shoulder. Fanny Kaplan, half blind, a Socialist Revolutionary who served eleven years at hard labour under the tsar, is arrested that evening and says she did it. He survives. She is shot in a courtyard behind the Kremlin on the third of September without a trial, and the Red Terror is decreed the same week.
suggested_refs: The commemorative stone and the 1947 Merkurov bust on the site of the Michelson works
The decree on the Red Terror, 5 September 1918
sources: ru.wikipedia, Moscow Electromechanical Plant named after Vladimir Ilyich (former Michelson works)

stops.name: The Kremlin, the Third International
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding congress of the Communist International, held in the Kremlin in Moscow, 2-6 March 1919. The pool's entry was headed Smolny and Petrograd while carrying Moscow coordinates, which is corrected here.
stops.campa: Fifty-one delegates, most of them already in Moscow because the blockade will not let them home, meet in a small hall inside the Kremlin for five days in March and constitute a Third International against the Second, which he holds to have died in August 1914, on the day its parties voted their governments the war credits. The revolutions this new International exists to coordinate are the ones in Berlin, Munich, and Budapest. Within the year all three are dead. The headquarters stays in Moscow, and so does the money.
suggested_refs: The founding congress of the Communist International, Kremlin, 2-6 March 1919

stops.name: The Kremlin, the dreamer in the Kremlin
stops.date_confidence: attested. The meeting is recorded in h_g_wells.journey.json at this pin, which is inherited byte-identically: Wells was brought to Moscow by Maxim Gorky, given an hour in a small office in the Kremlin in October 1920, and wrote the visit up in Russia in the Shadows the same year. The electrification quotation is from a speech of 21 November 1920, a month after the interview.
stops.campa: H. G. Wells, brought to Moscow by Gorky and given an hour in a small office inside the Kremlin, finds a short man with a flicker in his eyes who wants to talk about electricity. The whole of Russia, dark and wooden and roadless and largely illiterate, is to be rebuilt on electric power. Wells writes futures for a living and cannot make himself believe this one; he goes home and calls the man the dreamer in the Kremlin. The state plan for electrification is published that December. Thirty power stations in ten to fifteen years, in a country where the tram lines have stopped.
stops.quote: Communism is Soviet power plus the electrification of the whole country, since industry cannot be developed without electrification.
stops.quote_source: Speech to the Moscow Gubernia Conference of the RCP(b), 21 November 1920, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: H. G. Wells, Russia in the Shadows (1920)
The GOELRO state electrification plan, December 1920

stops.name: Moscow, the congress and the ice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Kronstadt rebellion of 1-18 March 1921 and its suppression under Tukhachevsky, and for the Tenth Party Congress sitting concurrently in Moscow, where the New Economic Policy and the ban on factions were adopted. Lenin was in Moscow and not at Kronstadt, which is why the stop is staged here rather than at the fortress at 59.9917 / 29.7728. The day orders the congress.
stops.campa: The war is won and the country is finished: industry at a fraction of 1913, the cities emptying back into the villages, risings across Tambov and the Volga, and on the first of March the sailors of Kronstadt, the men who made October, demanding soviets without Bolsheviks in them. The Tenth Congress opens in Moscow while the ice is still hard enough to march an army over. Delegates leave the hall in their hundreds to go and storm the fortress. In their absence the congress abolishes grain requisition and legalises private trade. It also bans factions inside the party. Both measures pass that week. The fortress falls on the eighteenth.
suggested_refs: The Kronstadt programme of 1 March 1921 and its suppression, 18 March 1921
The Tenth Congress resolutions on the tax in kind and on party unity
sources: Standard party history for the Tenth Congress, not re-verified

segments.name: Gorki: the Strokes and the Letter

stops.name: Gorki, the right side stops answering
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from standard biographical consensus for the first stroke of May 1922, its aphasia and right-sided weakness; the exact day is the one usually given and is not independently confirmed here. The estate coordinate is the correct one for Gorki Leninskiye; the pool's afterlife lens carried 55.4058 / 37.8342, some 12 km southeast, contradicting its own geography lens.
stops.campa: The estate south of Moscow belonged to a general's widow and was nationalised with its furniture, its glasshouses, and its telephone. He is sent out there to rest, and rest is the one instruction he has never been able to follow. On the twenty-sixth of May the right side stops answering and the words will not come; for weeks he cannot say the simplest nouns and is taught them back one at a time, like a child. One of Kaplan's bullets is still in his neck. By autumn he is well enough to return to the Kremlin and work eleven-hour days. In December it happens again.
suggested_refs: The Gorki estate, nationalised 1918 and used for Lenin's convalescences

stops.name: Gorki, the letter to the congress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the dictation of the Letter to the Congress from late December 1922 and for the addendum of 4 January 1923 proposing Stalin's removal as General Secretary. The Krupskaya telephone incident as the immediate trigger is standard biography and not independently confirmed. The Politburo's restrictions on his reading and visitors are attested in outline.
stops.campa: Half paralysed, forbidden by his own Politburo to read the newspapers or receive reports, allowed a stenographer for a few minutes a day, he dictates a short document addressed to the party congress that will meet after him. It weighs the six men who might succeed him and finds a fault in each. Ten days later he adds a postscript about the General Secretary's manners, having learned that Stalin has sworn at Krupskaya down the telephone for taking his dictation. The pages go into envelopes marked to be opened by him alone, or after his death, by Nadezhda Konstantinovna.
stops.quote: I suggest that the comrades think about a way of removing Stalin from that post and appointing another man in his stead who in all other respects differs from Comrade Stalin in having only one advantage, namely, that of being more tolerant, more loyal, more polite and more considerate to the comrades, less capricious, etc.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Congress (the Testament), addendum of 4 January 1923, Marxists Internet Archive
suggested_refs: The reading of the Testament to regional delegations at the Thirteenth Party Congress, May 1924, under rules barring notes and open discussion

stops.name: Gorki, the last winter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death at Gorki on 21 January 1924 at 18:50, aged 53, after falling into a coma, and for the autopsy finding of severe sclerosis; the brain was removed and sectioned for study in 1925. The third stroke of 10 March 1923 and the removal to Gorki on 15 May 1923 are carried at reconstruction from standard consensus.
stops.campa: The third stroke, in March 1923, takes nearly all his speech; he is moved out to Gorki in May and does not leave it again. Photographs from that summer show a man in a wicker chair on a terrace, looking at the camera. He is taught a few words back and loses them again. On the twenty-first of January 1924, at ten minutes to seven in the evening, having fallen into a coma, he dies at fifty-three. The autopsy finds the arteries of the brain so hardened by sclerosis that the physicians remark on it in writing.
suggested_refs: The 1924 autopsy protocol and the 1925 sectioning of the brain by Oskar Vogt and Soviet colleagues
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Death and state funeral of Vladimir Lenin'

segments.name: The Body That Was Not Buried

stops.name: The Hall of Columns, four days of queue
stops.date_confidence: attested that the body was brought to Moscow by train and lay in state in the Hall of Columns of the House of Trade Unions from 23 to 27 January 1924, and that the Funeral Commission was renamed the Commission for the Immortalization of the Memory of Vladimir Ulyanov Lenin. The family's objections, including Krupskaya's, and the reported wish for burial beside his mother in Petrograd are attested. Crowd figures are approximate; coordinates approximate for the building on Bolshaya Dmitrovka.
stops.campa: The coffin comes up to Moscow by train and is carried into a ballroom of the old Nobles' Assembly, under chandeliers, between white columns hung with red and black. The queue outside stands through four days and four nights in a cold near thirty below, bonfires burning along the pavement, and the people who pass the bier are counted in hundreds of thousands. What the family wants is a grave in Petrograd beside his mother. Before the funeral has taken place, the commission arranging it has renamed itself the Commission for the Immortalization of the Memory of Vladimir Ulyanov Lenin.
suggested_refs: Krupskaya's objection to the embalming and the family's request for ordinary burial
sources: europeanmemories.net, 'Lenin's Mausoleum: A Haunted House on Red Square'

stops.name: Red Square, the glass case
stops.date_confidence: attested for the successive wooden structures, for Shchusev's permanent mausoleum in red granite, black and grey labradorite, marble and porphyry, completed October 1930, and for the Vorobiev and Zbarsky embalming method. Corrected against the pool on two points: the initial embalming was by Alexei Abrikosov, with Vorobiev and Zbarsky developing the long-term method afterwards, and the maintenance interval is given as yearly by the encyclopedic source and as eighteen months only by press accounts, so no number is stated here.
stops.campa: A wooden cube goes up against the Kremlin wall in three days, the frozen ground broken with dynamite, and a larger wooden one replaces it in the spring. Vorobiev and Zbarsky work out a chemistry that will hold a body against the ordinary course of decay for as long as anyone keeps paying for it. Shchusev builds the permanent thing in red granite, black labradorite and porphyry, finished in 1930. What the queue is shown is the face and the hands. A laboratory maintains everything else, re-treating the body on a schedule, and has done so without interruption ever since.
suggested_refs: Alexey Shchusev's mausoleum on Red Square, completed October 1930
The Mausoleum Lab and the Vorobiev-Zbarsky method
sources: europeanmemories.net, 'Lenin's Mausoleum: A Haunted House on Red Square'

stops.name: Kyiv, the statue on Shevchenko Boulevard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the felling of the Kyiv statue on 8 December 2013, for the monument counts, and for the Ukrainian decommunization law passed 9 April 2015 and signed 15 May 2015, under which 1,320 Lenin monuments had been dismantled by January 2017. The 2025 closure of the mausoleum for structural repair said to run to June 2027 is carried at reconstruction: it rests on a Reuters report the verification pass could not fetch.
stops.campa: On the eighth of December a crowd on Shevchenko Boulevard pulls down a Lenin of red Karelian quartzite that has stood there since 1946, and breaks it up on the pavement with sledgehammers; people carry pieces away in their pockets. Ukraine begins with more than five thousand of him and passes a law in 2015 giving six months for the rest. The state he made was dissolved in 1991 by the signatures of three republics. The body on Red Square is where the commission put it, and the mausoleum is shut for structural repair until 2027.
suggested_refs: The Ukrainian decommunization laws of April and May 2015
Nina Tumarkin, Lenin Lives! The Lenin Cult in Soviet Russia (1983, rev. 1997)
sources: Reuters, 10 June 2025, cited but unreachable at verification
